lessons.title: The same protocol, compiled: reading the C++ DUT
lessons.objective: Read cpp/ as a C++ engineer would — header/source split, what a translation unit is, and why RAII replaces the cleanup code you would otherwise have to remember to write.

blocks.text:
`cpp/` is the same DUT you have been testing all fortnight, written in C++.

The split is the first thing to read:

* **`include/dut/*.hpp`** — declarations. What exists, what it promises.
* **`src/*.cpp`** — definitions. Each `.cpp` is a **translation unit**: compiled alone into a `.o`, then linked together.

Python has no such step — `import` finds and executes source at runtime. C++ resolves everything before the program runs, which is why a typo in a rarely-taken branch fails your **build**, not your 3 a.m. test run.

The second thing to read is `Socket` in `server.hpp`: it owns one OS handle, closes it in its destructor, and deletes its copy constructor.
blocks.more:
Why deleting the copy constructor matters: an OS socket handle is a *resource with an owner*, and copying the wrapper would give you two owners that each close the same handle — a double close, which on a busy server can close some *other* connection that reused the number. Deleting copy and defining move makes that a compile error instead of a Tuesday-afternoon mystery.

This is RAII: Resource Acquisition Is Initialisation. Acquire in the constructor, release in the destructor, and the release happens on *every* exit path — normal return, early return, or a thrown exception unwinding the stack. It is the same idea as Python's `with` block and `LabClient.__exit__`, except you get it once at the type level instead of remembering a `with` at every use site.

Note also `handle_connection(Socket connection, ...)`: the socket is taken **by value** and moved into the thread, so that thread owns the handle and closes it however it exits. Ownership is written into the signature.

blocks.question: handle_connection() takes its Socket by value and the thread is detached. When does the socket get closed?
options: Never — a detached thread leaks its arguments
When handle_connection returns, by ~Socket() on the moved-in value
When the server shuts down and closes all sockets in a loop
Only if the client disconnects first
blocks.reveal: The parameter is an ordinary local object owned by that thread. Whichever way handle_connection leaves — falling off the end, an early `return` after send_failed, or an exception unwinding — the destructor runs and the handle is closed. Nothing in the code says "close", and nothing has to.

blocks.instructions:
Read the two files side by side and answer three questions from the source:

```code cpp/include/dut/server.hpp cpp/src/protocol.cpp simulator/simulator.py
```

1. In `protocol.cpp`, find `build_response()`. Compare it to `build_response()` in `simulator/simulator.py` — which error codes are produced, and in what order are the checks made?
2. In `server.hpp`, find `WinsockGuard`. What does its destructor do, and why is that a class rather than a `WSACleanup()` call at the end of main?
3. In `server.cpp`, find where `Socket connection(accepted);` becomes the thread's argument. Which line transfers ownership?

Then prove the two implementations really agree — build first if you have not yet:

```cmake -S cpp -B cpp/build
cmake --build cpp/build
```

blocks.description: Builds cpp/ with CMake and requires both the executable and the test binary to exist afterwards.

args.success_note: The C++ DUT compiled and linked. cpp/build/bin now holds a native executable built from the sources you just read.

blocks.description: Runs the parity suite: the same bytes are sent to both DUTs and the replies must match exactly.

args.success_note: Both DUTs answered byte-identically across every request shape, met the 250 ms deadline, and wrote the same evidence fields. The harness genuinely does not care which one it is driving.

blocks.question: Why can build_response() be tested by CTest without opening a socket?
options: CTest stubs out the network layer automatically
Because it is a pure function of its argument — no socket, no clock, no global state — so it lives in dut_core and the test binary links that library directly
Because the test binary runs the server in a background thread first
It cannot; the CTest cases start a real server on a random port
blocks.explanation: The same separation the Python DUT has: protocol logic is a pure function, so its whole contract is testable in microseconds, and only the parts that genuinely need a live process (sockets, threads, cleanup) require a running DUT. dut_tests links dut_core and calls the function; no port is ever bound.

blocks.question: The Python DUT never has to declare that it links against a socket library, but cpp/CMakeLists.txt says `target_link_libraries(dut_core PUBLIC ws2_32)` on Windows. What does that line do, and what error appears if you delete it?
blocks.sample_answer: It tells the linker to resolve the Winsock symbols (socket, bind, listen, recv…) against ws2_32. The compiler is happy without it — the declarations come from <winsock2.h> — so the failure appears only at link time as unresolved external symbols such as __imp_socket. Compilation checks that a name was declared; linking checks that it actually exists somewhere.

hints.text: Read the header before the source. A header is the promise; the .cpp is how the promise is kept.
Ownership questions are answered by signatures: `Socket(const Socket&) = delete;` means 'you may not copy me', and a by-value parameter plus std::move at the call site means 'you now own this'.

The ownership transfer is `std::thread(handle_connection, std::move(connection), ...)` in run_server — std::move turns the local Socket into an rvalue the thread's parameter can move-construct from, leaving the local one holding kInvalidSocket.
If the build fails with 'ninja: command not found' or no generator, run `cmake -S cpp -B cpp/build` first — that configure step is what writes the build files the --build step consumes.

lessons.title: CMake and CTest: configure, build, test
lessons.objective: Drive the native build yourself — configure, build, inspect the build directory, run CTest, and read a deliberately broken build's error the way you read a failing test.

blocks.text:
CMake is two commands, always in this order:

1. **Configure** — `cmake -S cpp -B cpp/build` reads `CMakeLists.txt`, finds a compiler, and writes build files into `cpp/build`.
2. **Build** — `cmake --build cpp/build` runs that generated build system.

`cpp/build/` is disposable. Everything in it is derived; deleting it costs you a rebuild and nothing else. That is why it is gitignored, and why "delete the build directory and configure again" is the correct first move when a build behaves impossibly.

`CMakeLists.txt` declares three targets: the library `dut_core`, the executable `dut`, and the test binary `dut_tests` — then registers each test case with `add_test`, which is what `ctest` runs.
blocks.more:
Targets, not files, are the unit CMake reasons about. `target_link_libraries(dut PRIVATE dut_core)` says the executable needs the library; `target_include_directories(dut_core PUBLIC include)` says that anything linking dut_core also inherits its include path — which is why `dut_tests` can `#include "dut/protocol.hpp"` without repeating a single path.

PRIVATE vs PUBLIC is the whole idea: PRIVATE is an implementation detail, PUBLIC propagates to consumers. Getting that wrong does not break your build — it breaks the build of whoever depends on you, later, which is the expensive kind of wrong.

`CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE` selects the flag set. This project defaults to Debug because the debugging module needs symbols; a release build (`-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release`) optimises and inlines, and inlined frames are exactly the ones missing from a backtrace when you need them most.

**Single-config vs multi-config generators** — the difference that bites first. Ninja and Makefiles are *single-config*: the build type is fixed at configure time by `CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE`. Visual Studio and Xcode are *multi-config*: one configure produces all of Debug/Release, and you choose per command — `cmake --build cpp/build --config Debug`, and crucially `ctest -C Debug`. Omit `-C` on a multi-config build and CTest cannot tell which binaries you meant, so every test reports `Not Run` rather than failing honestly. `-C Debug` is accepted and ignored by single-config generators, which is why every ctest command in this project carries it: one command line that works on both.

blocks.question: You edit cpp/src/protocol.cpp and run `cmake --build cpp/build`. What gets recompiled?
options: Every .cpp in the project — C++ has no incremental build
Only protocol.cpp, then dut_core, dut and dut_tests are relinked
Nothing until you re-run the configure step
Only protocol.cpp; the executables keep their old code until you delete cpp/build
blocks.reveal: The generated build system tracks per-object dependencies: one translation unit changed, so one object is rebuilt, and everything that links it is relinked. Editing a *header* is the expensive case — every translation unit that includes it is out of date.

blocks.instructions:
Run the full native cycle, then break it on purpose:

```cmake -S cpp -B cpp/build
cmake --build cpp/build
ctest --test-dir cpp/build -C Debug --output-on-failure
```

All seven tests should pass. If you drop the `-C Debug` and CMake chose a multi-config generator (Visual Studio), every test reports `Not Run — Test not available without configuration`; that is the generator difference in the expandable note, not a broken build.

Now look at what the build produced — `cpp/build/bin/` holds `dut` and `dut_tests`; `cpp/build/CMakeCache.txt` records the compiler and generator CMake chose. Find the `CMAKE_GENERATOR` line and see which one you got.

Next, cause a real compile error and read it. In `cpp/src/protocol.cpp`, delete the semicolon at the end of any statement inside `build_response`, rebuild, and read the message: file, line, column, and what the compiler expected. Then put it back and rebuild to green.

Finally run one CTest case by name and watch it fail-fast:

```ctest --test-dir cpp/build -C Debug -R protocol.invalid_json --output-on-failure
```

blocks.description: Runs the whole CTest suite and requires every registered case to pass — including the protocol cases that encode REQ-COM-001, REQ-PROTO-001 and REQ-PROTO-002 in C++.

args.success_note: CTest ran every registered case and all passed — the same requirement checks the Python suite makes, enforced at the native level.

blocks.description: Runs a single CTest case by regex, proving selective execution works and that the build in cpp/build is current.

args.success_note: One named case ran on its own — the CTest equivalent of passing a pytest node id.

blocks.question: A colleague reports that their build fails with an error in a file they never touched, and it started right after they switched branches. Why is 'delete cpp/build and configure again' a reasonable first move, and what does it cost?
blocks.sample_answer: Everything under cpp/build is derived, including CMakeCache.txt, which pins the compiler and options chosen at configure time. A branch switch can leave that cache describing a different source tree, so deleting it removes stale state rather than debugging it. The only cost is a full reconfigure plus rebuild — no source is at risk, because nothing in the build directory is source.

hints.text: Configure once, build many times. If a command complains about missing build files, you skipped the configure step.

ctest must be told where the build tree is: `--test-dir cpp/build`. Without it, ctest looks in the current directory and reports 'No tests were found'. If every test says `Not Run — Test not available without configuration`, add `-C Debug`.
To see what CTest would run without running it: `ctest --test-dir cpp/build -N`. That lists the case names registered by add_test in CMakeLists.txt.
If the configure step cannot find a compiler on Windows, pass one explicitly: `cmake -S cpp -B cpp/build -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=C:/dev/mingw64/bin/g++.exe`.

lessons.title: One harness, two DUTs
lessons.objective: Point the existing pytest harness at the native DUT with --dut cpp, and understand why the tests needed no changes to work against a different implementation.

blocks.text:
The harness now takes an option:

```pytest --dut cpp
```

Everything else is unchanged. `tests/test_status.py` and `tests/test_protocol.py` do not know which implementation answered them, because the only implementation-specific code in the whole suite is `dut_command()` in `conftest.py` — the argv that starts the process.

That is the payoff of testing **at the interface**. The tests assert on protocol behaviour, not on Python internals, so a rewrite in another language is a configuration change rather than a test rewrite.

This is exactly the simulated-DUT / real-DUT split you meet in a lab: same stimulus, same expectations, different thing under test.
blocks.more:
Look at what would have broken this. If a test had imported `simulator.simulator` and called `build_response()` directly, it would be testing the Python implementation, not the protocol — useful as a unit test, useless for parity. If a test had asserted on the exact Python dict ordering, or on a log line only the Python logger emits, the C++ DUT would fail for reasons that have nothing to do with correctness.

`tests/test_cpp_dut.py` goes one step further than "both pass": it sends the same bytes to both DUTs in the same test run and compares the **raw reply lines**. Decoding both to dicts and comparing those would pass even if one emitted `{"a":1}` and the other `{"a": 1}` — a difference that matters the moment something diffs logs or a stricter client parses the stream.

The skip is deliberate too: on a machine with no compiler these tests skip rather than fail, because an unbuilt DUT is a missing capability, not a defect.

blocks.question: You run `pytest --dut cpp` on a machine where cpp/build was never built. What happens?
options: Every test fails with a connection error
The tests skip with a message telling you to build first
pytest falls back to the Python DUT silently
The run errors during collection
blocks.reveal: conftest.cpp_dut_path() returns None and the fixture calls pytest.skip with the build command. A skip says 'this machine cannot answer the question'; a failure would say 'the product is broken'. Reporting the second when you mean the first is how test suites lose their credibility.

blocks.instructions:
Drive the same tests against both implementations and compare the reports:

```pytest -v tests/test_status.py tests/test_protocol.py
pytest -v tests/test_status.py tests/test_protocol.py --dut cpp
```

The test ids are identical; only the process behind the socket changed.

Now look at how little made that possible — open `tests/conftest.py` and find `dut_command()`. Confirm for yourself that it is the *only* place the implementation is named, then check `tests/test_status.py` for any mention of Python, the simulator module, or an import of it (there is none).

Finally, run the parity suite that compares both at once:

```pytest -v tests/test_cpp_dut.py
```

blocks.description: Runs the requirement-linked protocol and status tests against the C++ DUT — the same node ids you have been running all along.

args.success_note: The unchanged requirement tests passed against the native DUT. The harness is implementation-agnostic in fact, not just in intention.

blocks.question: Which of these test styles would have blocked the switch to a C++ DUT?
options: Connecting to host/port and asserting on the JSON response
Importing simulator.simulator and calling build_response() directly in the test
Asserting that a status response arrives within 250 ms
Reading the DUT log file for a dut_ready line
blocks.explanation: Calling the Python function directly tests one implementation, not the protocol — there is no C++ equivalent to import. The other three describe externally observable behaviour that any conforming implementation must exhibit, which is why they survived the swap untouched. (Direct unit tests are still valuable — that is what cpp/tests and a pure-function test do — but they cannot double as parity tests.)

blocks.question: In a hardware lab you would run the same suite against a simulator and against real hardware. Which parts of a result would you trust equally from both, and which would you not?
blocks.sample_answer: Protocol and logic results transfer well: a malformed message rejected by the simulator should be rejected by the hardware, and a wrong error code is a real defect either way. Timing does not transfer — the simulator's 250 ms margin says nothing about bus latency, scheduling jitter, or I/O on the real device, so a passing timing test against a simulator is evidence about the harness, not about the hardware.

hints.text: The tests do not import the DUT. Ask yourself what they *do* depend on — a host, a port, and a protocol.
conftest.py::dut_command is the switch; the dut fixture calls it with whatever --dut selected, and everything downstream sees only a RunningDut.
Environment variable FTL_DUT=cpp does the same thing as --dut cpp, which is how CI can run the whole suite twice without editing any command line.
